items.headline: CoreWeave: customers now prepay up to 100%, and demand runs 10x capacity
items.summary: CoreWeave's Q3 call said customers are now funding up to 100% of contract value upfront, with qualified demand about ten times available capacity through 2027 and 2028 interest already several times what it has. @aleabitoreddit added that older Ampere and Hopper rental prices rose 30-50% quarter over quarter; @GavinSBaker says the shift from offtake financing to prepayments makes operating cash flow to EBITDA the metric that matters and shortens GPU payback. The stock rose more than 16% overnight.
items.short: CoreWeave says customers prepay up to 100% and demand is 10x capacity.

items.headline: TSMC calls leading-node demand "insatiable"
items.summary: Quoting TSMC at the Nikkei Forum, @aleabitoreddit reports the company sees no sign of an AI slowdown, says demand is still far above what it can supply, and names power and substrates as customers' bottlenecks. On its mid-to-high-50s growth estimate for AI accelerator revenue through 2029, C.C. Wei said it "probably will be higher."
items.short: TSMC says AI chip demand is still far above its supply.

items.headline: Nvidia erases Tuesday's drop amid the Huang story
items.summary: @KobeissiLetter reports Nvidia rose more than 6% as investors bought the dip, erasing the prior day's decline tied to the Jensen Huang reporting, while Nasdaq 100 futures climbed about 1.5% on CoreWeave's results.

items.headline: SpaceX is building Kessel, a custom Vera Rubin rack for Earth and orbit
items.summary: @SemiAnalysis_ says SpaceX is developing Kessel, a custom Vera Rubin NVL72 rack that swaps the internal NVLink cable cartridges for a passive PCB midplane, keeping 72 GPU packages, 18 compute trays and 9 switch trays arranged back-to-back. It is designed for both terrestrial and orbital deployment; the open question is whether the smaller design makes a midplane practical.
items.short: SpaceX's Kessel rack is designed for both ground and orbital data centers.

items.author: Fireside Alpha
items.text:
Ex-Tesla President Jon McNeill reveals Elon Musk's idea for Neuralink started in the back of a Model S in Hong Kong, with Elon asking how fast he could type.

Elon Musk then asked for the top brain-computer interface researchers’ papers on the spot, and met them the next week:

“Elon and I were traveling together to China. We just landed in Hong Kong. We’re in the back of a Model S, and we’re both catching up on our inbox on our phones. And he looks over at me and says, how fast can you type with your thumbs?”

“And I said, I have no idea. I’ve never timed it. He’s like, well, the average human’s 18 words a minute. He said, how fast can you type on a keyboard? I said, I think it’s like 60 or 70 words a minute. So let’s call it 60.”

“He said, exactly. So you are more than three times faster on the keyboard than you are on your phone. This device has slowed the input into the machine. And he’s like, that’s a big deal, because you can’t get speed of answers and decision making if you’re going three times slower.”

“He’s like, what if you could think into the machine? I was like, well, that would blow this constraint away, because now we don’t have keyboards and thumbs to go through. You’re thinking in real time into the machine. He’s like, exactly. That would pull the front-end constraint off of the compute for humans. That’s a big deal.”

“So he didn’t sit on these ideas. He’s very unique in this way. And he said to his chief of staff, Sam Teller, who’s in the front seat: Sam, can you track down the top neuro computer science interface researchers in the world? Get their papers.”

“I want to read the papers while we’re here in China and on the flight back, and I want to meet with these people next week, because I want to start to work on brain-computer interface. And just like that, fast.”

“So by the next week, he’s meeting with some of the top minds in the world on this topic, and he doesn’t let go until he starts Neuralink.”

quoted.author: Fireside Alpha
quoted.text:
Bill Ackman says Neuralink and other brain-computer interfaces will let the blind see again within "not too many years"

“And you know, my daughter, who lost pretty much basic function, ability to walk, ability to speak, ability to see, is regaining function. She’s cognitively, as far as I can tell, fine. She’s relearning how to speak, and she’s learning again how to walk. And I’m confident we’re going to get her back."

"Biggest challenge right now is that the optic nerve damage from the pressure on the brain has caused her to lose probably 98% of her vision."

"But even there I’m optimistic. Spent a lot of time in the last few months meeting with all these brain computer interface companies, obviously Neuralink being the most famous, but there’s some other very promising lower intervention technologies."

"And this will be a period, you know, AI is going to enable us. We’re going to be able to get more signal from the brain, and we’re going to be able to interpret that signal much more effectively than we had before. And the blind will see again, and people who have not been able to walk, so to speak, paraplegics, I believe will walk again. It’s a matter of not months but years, but not too many years.”

items.author: a16z
items.text:
HubSpot co-founder and CTO Dharmesh Shah says it's less scary to build an AI startup now than in 2023, as long as you stay off the Yellow Brick Road the frontier labs are following:

"The frontier model companies have invested hundreds of billions of dollars building, doing the pre-training. And so their whole business effectively now is taking the capex that they've spent and the money they're continuing to spend and saying, 'How do we sell inference? How do we sell tokens? How do we monetize the thing that we've built?'"

"There are SaaS companies and startups that know their particular domain, know their market, have some distribution, or have something that allows them to sell tokens and be a reseller of inference."

"Think of AI as infrastructure in the same way we thought of AWS and cloud infrastructure 15 years ago... I think it's less scary now to build in and around the AI arena than it was in 2023."

"We have open source. We have lots of great commercial products. So as long as you stay off the Yellow Brick Road, it is completely possible now that you're not gonna get margined out, because you have options."

@dharmesh

items.author: Oguz Erkan
items.text:
This is probably the most bullish signal for neoclouds like $CRWV and $NBIS.

At the beginning of the year, neocloud long-term contract prices were around $10 million per MW, while short-term, large-scale prices were around $40 million per MW.

The thesis was that high short-term prices would inevitably raise long-term pricing, which was an optionality the market didn't price for neoclouds.

We are seeing this play out as $CRWV long-term pricing effectively doubled this year. It's not a thesis anymore; it's the reality, but the market still hasn't priced it.

Couldn't be more bullish.

items.title: The last time @GavinSBaker and I sat down to record a podcast
items.author: David George
items.summary: David George recaps his second a16z conversation with Gavin Baker on where the AI cycle stands. Baker has spent the summer asking operators for one metric that is getting worse and has not found one, while AI revenue still rests on fewer than 10 million heavy users against roughly 1.5 billion knowledge workers. The argument: supply is short and the market is positive-sum, with room for labs, open models, clouds, enterprises and apps to win.

items.title: Gavin Baker on orbital compute
items.author: Invest Like the Best
items.summary: Gavin Baker argues data centers in space are the most important thing of the next three to four years: constant sun means no batteries and cooling is free. He points to SpaceX's GPU clusters, share of mass to orbit and constellation, and estimates Starship could lift 10 to 15 megawatts to sun-synchronous orbit per flight.

items.headline: CoreWeave targets adjusted profit in early 2028
items.summary: Q3 revenue rose nearly 170% to $3.66 billion, above estimates, and backlog reached $132.5 billion. The company raised 2026 revenue guidance to $13.0-13.3 billion, said it will not tap unsecured debt at current yields, and expects about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months.
items.short: CoreWeave beat estimates and expects adjusted profit in the first half of 2028.

items.headline: Oral GLP-1 pill cut sleep-apnea episodes in a year-long trial
items.summary: In two ATTAIN-OSA trials of 712 adults with moderate-to-severe sleep apnea and excess weight, daily orforglipron cut breathing interruptions by about 18 events an hour versus about five on placebo, with 10-11% weight loss and lower blood pressure and CRP. Results were presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions.
items.short: Daily orforglipron reduced sleep apnea and weight in two trials.

items.headline: Blocking one microRNA reversed heart scarring in AFib models
items.summary: Baylor and Oxford researchers designed a blocker that stops microRNA-31-5p from hitting the calcitonin receptor; in mice it reversed established atrial fibrosis by about 30% and reduced abnormal heart rhythms, and it worked in cells from AFib patients. Published in Nature Cardiovascular Research.
items.short: A microRNA blocker reversed atrial scarring in mice.

items.title: Four Cards
items.rule: If a card is red on one side, it has a circle on the other.
items.explanation: Red could hide something that breaks the rule; Triangle breaks it if the other side turns out to be Red. Circle can't break it (the rule never says only those cards have it), and Green isn't covered by the rule at all. Most people pick the card that matches the rule's second half instead of the one that could falsify it.

items.text:
The American middle class was built in part on people getting their foot in the door.

An entry-level job.

A decent paycheck.

A chance to learn.

A promotion.

Eventually, a home and a family.

Now companies are discovering they can automate some of the work that used to give young people their start.
